analysis.one_liner: Lets victims of gender-motivated violence sue negligent employers when a violent crime happens on their premises.
analysis.headline: The bill died without a single hearing or vote, referred to two House committees with no cosponsors before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would give victims of violent crimes committed because of gender the right to sue, in federal or state court, any employer whose careless conduct allowed the crime to happen on the employer's property. It covers businesses whose operations touch interstate commerce, allows compensatory and punitive damages, and does not require a prior criminal conviction. It also directs the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission to write guidance helping employers avoid liability through safety policies.
analysis.who_benefits: Victims of gender-motivated violent crimes, who gain a new federal civil right to sue and recover damages from an employer whose negligence let the crime occur on the employer's premises; they need only prove the crime was gender-motivated by a preponderance of the evidence, and they need no prior criminal case.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a federal cause of action letting an injured party recover compensatory and punitive damages, plus injunctive relief, from an employer whose negligent conduct resulted in a gender-motivated crime of violence on premises the employer controls [S2] [S3].
Victims would not need a prior criminal complaint, prosecution, or conviction to bring a claim, lowering the barrier to civil relief [S2] [S3].
Federal and state courts would both be able to hear these cases, so victims could sue in whichever forum is more accessible [S2] [S3].
The EEOC would be required to create materials for employers on personnel policies and safety standards to help prevent gender-motivated violence in the first place [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Businesses with premises where gender-motivated violence occurs despite their negligence — including hospitality, retail, and other interstate-commerce employers — would face new liability, and their insurers would bear claim costs; some of that cost would likely be passed to customers through premiums and prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill would impose a new negligence-based liability on any employer whose business touches interstate commerce, meaning hotels, bars, restaurants, retailers, and other property-controlled businesses could face jury-awarded punitive damages even where no criminal case was ever brought [S2] [S3].

Critics of similar federal civil-rights-remedy laws argue Congress overreaches by regulating local crime under its commerce power; the Supreme Court struck down the civil-remedy provision of the Violence Against Women Act on those grounds in 2000 (widely reported, not in the provided sources).

Because liability does not require a prior conviction, employers could face expensive federal litigation over allegations of gender-motivated violence that a court never confirmed as criminal conduct [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill gives victims a targeted, limited remedy: it excludes random violence unrelated to gender and requires the victim to show the crime was gender-motivated. That limits suits against businesses, but the threat of punitive damages with no criminal-conviction requirement would still create substantial litigation exposure for hospitality and other customer-facing employers, some of it passed on to consumers. The EEOC guidance requirement partially offsets that by pushing employers toward preventive policies.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced, less than four months before the Congress ended, and neither committee ever considered it; it died there without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.

narrative.text: Rep. Carolyn Maloney of New York introduced the bill on September 17, 2008, near the end of the 110th Congress [S1] [S3].
It was referred to both the Education and Labor Committee and the Judiciary Committee, the standard route for a bill touching labor and civil-rights law [S3] [S5].
No other member cosponsored the bill, and no committee reported it, held a hearing, or brought it to the floor before the Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and their liability insurers, who avoided any new federal negligence liability for gender-motivated violence on their premises; victims gained nothing.

against.what_they_did: Received the referral on introduction and never took it up — no markup, hearing, or report.

sides.party_line_note: There was never any vote or public position from other members; the only record of support is the single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors, so no partisan pattern can be read from the record.

industries.industry: Interstate-commerce employers with customer or employee premises (hotels, bars, restaurants, retailers)
industries.note: The bill would make them liable in damages when negligent conduct lets a gender-motivated violent crime happen on their property, and it caps that exposure only with the gender-motivation requirement. Their interest in avoiding new liability ran directly against victims' interest in a remedy.

A new federal tort cause of action with punitive damages would raise claim payouts and premiums, costs partly passed to customers. Insurers were never recorded as taking a position, but the bill's liability scheme bears on them directly.

industries.industry: Victims' rights and anti-violence advocacy community
industries.note: A federal civil remedy after the Supreme Court invalidated the VAWA civil-rights provision was a long-standing goal of this community; the bill would have restored a partial route to damages. No advocacy group position appears in the record.
